scenarios.scenario: Quarterly security pass: about 400 route handler files each need the identical audit step for missing authorization checks, every finding must be adversarially verified before it is reported, and next quarter the whole pass should rerun the same way from a single command.

key.primary: Dynamic workflow: a script fans out one auditor subagent per file, a verifier stage cross-checks findings, and the run is saved to .claude/workflows/ as a reusable slash command
key.rejected_alternative: Spawning many parallel subagents directly from the main conversation
key.rejection_reason: The main agent coordinates subagents turn by turn and every result returns to its context window; at 400 items that exceeds what one conversation can coordinate (20 concurrent subagents and 200 per session by default), and the orchestration is not repeatable. The workflow runtime runs dozens to hundreds of agents per run (up to 1,000, 16 concurrent), keeps intermediate results in script variables instead of any context window, and a saved run reruns as /<name>. This is the docs' own 'audit many files for the same issue' shape.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (each spawned agent has its own context; intermediate results live in script variables, and only the final report reaches the session)
key.lifecycle: explicit invocation: 'use a workflow' or the ultracode keyword in a typed prompt, later the saved /<name> command; a launch approval prompt gates the run per permission mode
key.failure_mode: Stopping mid fan-out is expensive on resume: cached results stop at the first unfinished agent and every agent started after it reruns; exiting Claude Code forfeits resume entirely (resume works only within the same session); no mid-run user input is possible.
key.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans only; on Pro it must be enabled from the Dynamic workflows row in /config

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: Claude writes a JavaScript orchestration script (invoked with `ultracode` or a plain 'use a workflow' request) that discovers the handler files, fans out one `agent()` per file through `pipeline()`, then runs an adversarial verification phase over the findings. Once the run is right, press `s` in `/workflows` to save the script into `.claude/workflows/` so next quarter it reruns as a single project slash command.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents fanned out turn by turn by the main agent. Rejected because 400 delegations plus a verify pass outgrow what one conversation can coordinate, every intermediate finding would land in the main context window, and nothing about the orchestration itself would be repeatable next quarter.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns it: the workflow runtime executes the script deterministically, so the per-file fan-out, the verification stage and the concurrency caps are code, not model judgment. The model only authors the script and supplies the audit reasoning inside each spawned agent.
sheets.context_boundary: The script runs in an isolated runtime separate from the conversation, and each spawned agent gets its own context window. Per-file audit results live in script variables; only the value the script returns (the verified finding list) crosses into the main session's context.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs when the saved command is invoked, or when the keyword or a natural-language workflow request appears in a prompt you typed yourself. It runs in the background until the script returns, you stop it with `x`, or a runtime cap trips; it is resumable only inside the same session, and exiting Claude Code makes the next session start it fresh.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on substance: the script guarantees every file gets an auditor, but whether an auth gap is actually spotted is still model judgment, and a missed finding is silent. Operationally, there is no mid-run user input, shell or MCP calls outside your allowlist can stall a long run on a permission prompt, and stopping mid fan-out reruns every agent that started after the first unfinished one.
sheets.version_caveat: Dynamic workflows need Claude Code v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan (on Pro you must switch on the Dynamic workflows row in `/config`); an org can kill them with `disableWorkflows` in managed settings or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1`. Watch the caps and the size guideline: 16 concurrent agents and 1,000 agents per run, and `workflowSizeGuideline` defaults to `medium` (under 15 agents) from v2.1.219, which will undersize a 400-file pass unless you set `large` or `unrestricted`.

sheets.primary: Dynamic workflow: a JavaScript orchestration script saved to .claude/workflows/audit-routes.js and invoked as /audit-routes, fanning one auditor agent per route file through pipeline() and passing every finding through a second adversarial verifier stage before it is reported. The file list is built outside the script (globbed and passed in as args, or returned by a first-stage agent) because the script itself has no filesystem access.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Skill plus subagent fan-out, with the model delegating roughly 400 audits turn by turn. It loses because the model re-decides the plan on every turn, so the per-file coverage and the mandatory verification gate drift between this quarter and next, and every intermediate finding lands in the main context window.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. A workflow runtime executes the script, so the fan-out, the per-file loop and the mandatory verify stage are code rather than model judgment; the model owns only the judgment inside each agent prompt, and the subagents the workflow spawns always run in acceptEdits mode with your tool allowlist regardless of the session permission mode.
sheets.context_boundary: The script runs in the workflow runtime, isolated from the conversation, and each spawned agent has its own context window. Intermediate audit findings live in script variables, so only the final returned array crosses back into the caller's context.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs when the saved /audit-routes command is invoked (the first authoring run comes from an explicit 'use a workflow' or ultracode opt-in), and stops when the script returns. A stopped run is resumable within the same session, but exiting Claude Code makes the next session start it fresh.
sheets.failure_mode: It fails partially open and quietly: the run is capped at 1,000 agents total and 16 concurrent, and 400 files across an audit stage plus a verify stage is 800 invocations, so growth in the route count silently collides with the cap. A failed agent resolves to null instead of throwing, so an unfiltered result set reports fewer routes audited without ever saying so, and there is no mid-run user input, so a bad run can only be stopped from /workflows.
sheets.version_caveat: Dynamic workflows require Claude Code v2.1.154 or later and are available on all paid plans plus the Anthropic API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry; on Pro they must be switched on from the Dynamic workflows row in /config. An organization can remove the mechanism entirely with "disableWorkflows": true in managed settings or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1.

sheets.primary: A project skill (SKILL.md under .claude/skills) that owns the audit procedure and fans out one read-only auditor subagent per file or small batch, then routes every candidate finding to a separate adversarial verifier subagent before it is allowed into the report. The skill file is the durable artifact that makes next quarter's rerun identical from one invocation.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Rejected because 400 audits are independent and need no peer negotiation; the team's messaging substrate adds coordination cost and cross-talk with no benefit here.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. A skill is instructions the model elects to follow, and nothing in the harness forces the adversarial verification gate. If the gate must be non-negotiable, back it with a hook (PreToolUse or Stop) that refuses a report lacking verifier verdicts.
sheets.context_boundary: The orchestrating context holds only the skill body, the file queue, and the merged findings. Each auditor and each verifier runs in its own subagent window; only a structured finding list or verdict crosses back. Raw route handler source never enters the main conversation.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs when the user invokes the skill by name or the description matches the request, and ends when the queue drains and the report is written. It has no standing effect between quarters: the file persists, the behaviour does not.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and is advisory. The realistic failures are silent partial coverage (the model shrinks 400 files to the ones it sampled and reports as if complete) and a verification pass that checks the summary rather than the code, because subagent reports lose the underlying evidence. Neither failure announces itself.
sheets.version_caveat: Skills with SKILL.md frontmatter are generally available in current Claude Code, and plugin packaging plus per-skill allowed-tools are more recent additions. I do not know the exact minimum version for any of these, nor the current cap on concurrently dispatched subagents, so the fan-out width may be silently throttled.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: a JavaScript orchestration script Claude writes that fans out one auditor subagent per route file with pipeline(), then runs a second phase where independent agents adversarially verify each finding before it is reported. Save that run's script from /workflows with 's' into .claude/workflows/ so next quarter the whole pass reruns as a single /<name> command.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that fans out subagents. A skill only makes the instructions repeatable, not the orchestration: Claude re-decides the plan turn by turn on every run, and 400 per-file results would land in the conversation's own context window rather than in script variables.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the script, so the script decides what runs next instead of Claude's turn-by-turn judgment, and the verification phase is a code-level stage rather than a request. Claude still authors the script, so plan quality stays model-owned even though execution is harness-owned.
sheets.context_boundary: The runtime executes the script in an isolated environment separate from your conversation. Each spawned auditor and verifier has its own context window, per-file findings live in script variables, and only the final returned report crosses into your session.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts when you invoke the saved /<name> command, or the first time by asking for a workflow or using the ultracode keyword, and runs in the background while the session stays responsive. It ends when the script returns, when a runtime cap is hit, or when you stop it from /workflows with 'x'; resume works only inside the same session, since exiting Claude Code makes the next session start the run fresh.
sheets.failure_mode: Bounded but expensive at this size: 16 concurrent agents and 1,000 agents per run, and stopping mid fan-out replays every agent that started after the first unfinished one even if it already completed. It fails open on scope and safety: the size guideline is advice not a cap, the Large workflow warning is advisory only, and the workflow's subagents always run in acceptEdits with file edits auto-approved regardless of your session permission mode.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan; on Pro you must turn on the Dynamic workflows row in /config. It can be switched off per user with disableWorkflows or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WORKFLOWS=1 and org-wide in managed settings, and the saved-script symlink check only landed in v2.1.216.

scenarios.scenario: A production service drops the connection after exactly one message and nobody knows why. I want five investigators working in parallel, each owning a different hypothesis, actively trying to disprove each other's theories like a scientific debate, with whatever consensus survives written to a findings doc.

key.primary: Agent team: a lead session spawns five teammates who share a task list and message each other directly through their mailboxes
key.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents launched from the main conversation
key.rejection_reason: Subagents only report results back to the agent that spawned them and never talk to each other, so the adversarial cross-examination cannot happen; each investigator would anchor on its own theory with no one challenging it. Teammates are full independent sessions with direct inter-agent messaging, and the competing-hypotheses debate is the documented flagship team use case: the theory that survives active disproof attempts is more likely the real root cause.
key.context_boundary: independent sessions (each teammate is a full Claude Code session with its own context window)
key.lifecycle: explicit spawn request in the prompt, or Claude proposes teammates and the user confirms; requires the experimental env flag set at session start
key.failure_mode: Task status can lag when a teammate fails to mark work complete, blocking dependents; the lead may declare the team finished early or start doing the work itself; in-process teammates do not survive /resume; token cost scales linearly with teammate count.
key.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default; requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment

sheets.primary: Agent team: the current session becomes the lead and spawns five named teammates, one per hypothesis, using peer messaging so each teammate actively tries to disprove the others' theories, with the surviving consensus written to the findings doc. This is the documented competing-hypotheses shape, where the debate itself is the mechanism that beats a single investigator's anchoring.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Dynamic workflow fanning out five investigator agents. It loses because workflow agents and subagents only return results to their caller and never message one another, so the cross-examination that the whole request is built on cannot happen while the investigation is still in flight.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness supplies the mailbox, the shared task list and file-locked task claiming, but nothing forces a teammate to genuinely attack a peer's hypothesis, and the lead approves teammate plans autonomously without prompting you. The only harness-side gates available are the TeammateIdle, TaskCreated and TaskCompleted hooks, which can exit 2 to push work back.
sheets.context_boundary: Each teammate is a full, independent Claude Code session with its own context window that loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills but not the lead's conversation history. What crosses the boundary is the spawn prompt going in, and peer messages, shared task-list state, idle notifications and the findings doc on disk coming back.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms when the first teammate is spawned, after you enable the feature and confirm the spawn; teammates then claim or are assigned tasks until they are asked to shut down or the session exits. Shutdown cleans up ~/.claude/teams/{team-name}/ automatically, while the task list under ~/.claude/tasks/ persists for resumed sessions.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory, and it degrades by stalling rather than erroring: teammates can stop on errors instead of recovering, task status lags so dependent tasks stay blocked, and the lead can declare the debate finished before the work is done. Five independent sessions also multiply token cost linearly, and /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates.
sheets.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default; they require CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment, without which no team is set up and Claude will not spawn teammates. The implicit spawn-and-auto-cleanup lifecycle described here is v2.1.178 and later, where TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist, and mailbox handling only recovers from a malformed entry from v2.1.207.

sheets.primary: An agent team: enable teams, then have the lead spawn five teammates, each owning one hypothesis, with the spawn prompt telling them to message each other and try to disprove each other's theories, and to update a findings doc with the surviving consensus. This is the documented debugging-with-competing-hypotheses pattern, where the debate structure is the mechanism that defeats anchoring.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents. They run inside one session, report results back to the main agent only, and never message each other, so the adversarial cross-examination that makes a surviving theory trustworthy cannot happen.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead decides who investigates what, when the debate has converged, and when to write the doc; teammates self-claim tasks from a shared list. The only harness-level levers are the TeammateIdle, TaskCreated and TaskCompleted hooks, which can exit with code 2 to keep a teammate working or block a premature completion.
sheets.context_boundary: Each teammate is a separate Claude Code session with its own context window. It loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills like a normal session plus the lead's spawn prompt, but not the lead's conversation history. What crosses between agents is mailbox messages, the shared task list, idle notifications to the lead, and the findings doc on disk.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate, which you approve, and is scoped to that one session. Teammates stop on a shutdown request they may reject, when you press 'x', or at session exit, which removes the team config directory automatically while the task list directory persists under cleanupPeriodDays.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open and talkative. Task status can lag so a completed task never unblocks its dependents, the lead may declare the investigation finished before it is, teammates sometimes stop on errors instead of recovering, and shutdown is slow because each finishes its current tool call. Five parallel sessions also multiply token cost linearly, and /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates.
sheets.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default; you must set CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1 in settings.json or the environment or no team is set up at all. The documented behaviour is as of v2.1.178, where TeamCreate and TeamDelete no longer exist and team_name in hook payloads is deprecated, and mailbox resilience to a malformed entry only arrived in v2.1.207.

sheets.primary: An agent team: the main session becomes the lead and spawns five teammates, each given one hypothesis in its spawn prompt, with an explicit instruction to message each other and try to disprove each other's theories. They coordinate through the shared task list and their mailboxes, and the surviving consensus is written to a findings doc on disk that the lead maintains.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents. Rejected because subagents only report back to the agent that spawned them and can never talk to each other, so the adversarial cross-examination that is the whole point here is structurally impossible.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead decides who to spawn, what to assign, when the debate has converged and what goes in the findings doc; the harness only supplies the mailbox files, the file-locked shared task list and the optional `TeammateIdle` / `TaskCompleted` hooks (exit code 2) that can push a teammate to keep working.
sheets.context_boundary: Each teammate is a full independent Claude Code session with its own context window, loading CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills from project and user settings but not the lead's conversation history. What crosses is the spawn prompt, direct `SendMessage` traffic between agents, shared task state, idle notifications, and the findings doc itself as a durable on-disk artifact.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms when the lead spawns the first teammate (you approve the spawn), and teammates run until they are asked to shut down, stopped with `x`, or the lead's session exits. The team config directory is removed at session end while the task list persists; `/resume` and `/rewind` do not restore in-process teammates, so a resumed session has to respawn them.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open. Nothing enforces that a hypothesis is genuinely falsified, so the team can converge on a consensus that is merely the loudest theory; teammates sometimes stop on API errors or fail to mark tasks complete, which blocks dependent tasks, and the lead often declares the investigation finished before the work is done. Token cost scales linearly with teammate count.
sheets.version_caveat: Agent teams are experimental and disabled by default: you must set `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` in settings.json or the environment, otherwise no team is set up and Claude will not spawn teammates. The documented behaviour is as of v2.1.178 (the old `TeamCreate` / `TeamDelete` tools no longer exist and `team_name` is deprecated); before v2.1.207 one malformed mailbox entry blocked delivery for that agent entirely.

sheets.primary: An agent team: five teammates in one shared team session, each chartered with a different hypothesis and able to message the others so rebuttals land while the work is in flight, with the lead writing the surviving consensus to a findings document.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Parallel subagents dispatched with the Task tool. Rejected because subagents cannot see or answer each other, so you would get five isolated monologues and no disproof.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness supplies the team substrate (separate contexts, message passing, addressability); whether the investigators genuinely attack each other's theories rather than politely agree is model behaviour driven by the charters.
sheets.context_boundary: Each teammate has its own context window. What crosses is the messages they post to each other plus their final reports; your main conversation should see the lead's synthesis and the findings doc, not five full investigation transcripts.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts when the team is created for this investigation and runs until the members converge or you stop them. It is a session-scoped construct, not standing configuration, so nothing about it survives into the next debugging session unless you re-create it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. The dominant failure is sycophantic convergence: five instances of the same model tend to agree rather than falsify, so a wrong consensus can be produced confidently. Secondary costs are roughly five times the tokens and a lead that summarizes the debate instead of the evidence.
sheets.version_caveat: Agent teams are the newest of these mechanisms and I believe they shipped as an opt-in or experimental feature. I do not know the exact version that introduced them, the setting or flag name that enables them, or whether availability is plan restricted.

scenarios.scenario: Running our test suite prints tens of thousands of lines. I want the suite run and only the failing tests with their error messages reported back, and the raw output must never enter the conversation I am working in.

key.primary: One subagent: delegate the test run so the verbose output stays in the subagent's own context and only the failure summary returns
key.rejection_reason: This is a single self-contained side task where only the result matters, the exact case the subagent docs name under 'isolate high-volume operations'. A workflow adds a launch approval prompt, a background runtime, and generated script scaffolding to run what is effectively one agent; the workflow docs reserve the mechanism for jobs that outgrow a handful of subagents or need the plan held in code. Scale machinery buys nothing here.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (subagent transcript is a separate file and window; only the final report returns to the caller)
key.lifecycle: model-decided delegation matched from the task description, or guaranteed for one task with an @-mention
key.failure_mode: The returned report still lands in the main context, so a poorly instructed subagent can return a huge result and defeat the isolation; background subagents (the default) also run with a reduced built-in tool set.
key.version_caveat: none (subagents run in the background by default as of v2.1.198)

sheets.primary: A subagent: a test-runner subagent definition with a narrow tool allowlist (shell plus read) and a cheap model, whose system prompt says to run the suite and return only failing test names with their error messages. The main agent delegates the run to it, either by description match or by an explicit 'use the test-runner subagent' instruction.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill (or slash command) that tells Claude to run the suite and report only failures. Rejected because a skill is instructions the main agent follows in the main conversation, so the tens of thousands of raw lines enter the working context window before any filtering happens, which is exactly the outcome being ruled out.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, and this is the point of the choice: the harness owns the boundary, because a subagent genuinely runs in a separate context window and only its final message returns. The model owns what it selects to put in that final message, and the model also owns the decision to delegate at all unless a hook forces it.
sheets.context_boundary: The raw suite output lives only in the subagent's own context window; the summary string it returns is the only thing that crosses into the main conversation. The subagent starts fresh with no main-session history (unless it is a forked subagent started with `/subtask`, which inherits the conversation instead).
sheets.lifecycle: It runs when the main agent delegates the task, and it ends when it returns its result. Run in the background it keeps going while the session continues and shows up in `/tasks` and the @-mention typeahead; it stops applying the moment the result is returned, and it has no standing effect on later turns.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on volume. The subagent decides how much detail to return, so a verbose return can still paste a wall of output back, and a very large run can overflow the subagent's own context and lose failures to truncation. Delegation itself is advisory: nothing stops the main agent from just running the suite inline, so a PreToolUse hook that blocks the raw test command in the main session is the only hard guarantee.
sheets.version_caveat: Subagents are generally available with no flag or plan gate; definitions resolve from project, user, plugin or CLI-defined scope. Note that as of v2.1.198 `/agents` no longer opens a management panel and just prints where the definition files live, so create or edit them by asking Claude or editing the files directly; a teammate inside an agent team also cannot launch a background subagent.

sheets.primary: A dedicated subagent (for example .claude/agents/test-runner.md) that runs the suite inside its own context window and returns only the failing test names with their error messages. Its final message is the only thing that crosses back.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A hook on the Bash tool that trims the test output. Rejected because the filtering needed here is judgment (deciding which lines constitute a failure and its message), which is model work, and I am not confident a PostToolUse hook can rewrite tool output that has already been produced.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the isolation: a subagent's context is genuinely separate and the parent receives only the returned report. The model owns what it chooses to put in that report, which is where the requirement can still be defeated.
sheets.context_boundary: The suite's tens of thousands of stdout lines live entirely in the subagent's window. Only one text report crosses into your conversation. The subagent's instructions must cap what it returns, since a verbose agent pasting a large excerpt would reintroduce exactly what you excluded.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires when you request a test run, or automatically when the agent description matches the request, and ends when the report is returned. Nothing persists between runs; the agent definition file persists, the context does not.
sheets.failure_mode: Closed with respect to the raw output (it structurally cannot leak) but open with respect to correctness. A subagent that misreads a crashed run can report 'all passed', and a huge log can exhaust the subagent's own context and force truncation or compaction that drops failures it already saw.
sheets.version_caveat: Subagents defined as .claude/agents Markdown files with name, description, tools and model frontmatter are generally available. I do not know which version introduced per-subagent model selection, and I do not know whether subagent output size is capped by the harness or only by the prompt.

sheets.primary: A subagent: a custom test-runner subagent definition with a narrow tool allowlist, invoked explicitly, that runs the suite in its own context window and returns only the failing test names and their error messages. This is the canonical case for a subagent, a side task whose output floods the main conversation and is never referenced again.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill executed in the main conversation. A /run-tests skill's steps run in your context window, so the tens of thousands of raw lines land in exactly the conversation you are trying to protect; only forking that work into a separate context solves it.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, but the model owns the outcome. The harness structurally guarantees the boundary, since a subagent gets a separate context window with its own input and output tokens, while whether Claude delegates at all and what its summary contains are interpreted instructions whose outcome can vary. Invoking the subagent explicitly rather than relying on description matching is what makes it reliable.
sheets.context_boundary: The suite runs entirely in the subagent's isolated context, which does not inherit your conversation history or invoked skills. Only the returned summary crosses back into your window, so the raw output never enters your session.
sheets.lifecycle: It is spawned on demand when you or Claude delegates the task, and it ends when it returns its summary. Finished subagents stay listed in /tasks for the session, but nothing about the run persists into later turns beyond that summary.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on volume. If Claude decides to run the suite itself in the main session instead of delegating, or the subagent pastes large output blocks into its summary, the raw output reaches you anyway; an instruction to report only failures is a request, not a guarantee. There is also no cheap follow-up, because a second question about the run means re-running the suite in a fresh context.
sheets.version_caveat: Subagents are generally available with no enabling flag or plan gate, but the surrounding commands moved: as of v2.1.198 /agents no longer opens a panel and only prints subagent file locations, so you create and edit definitions by asking Claude or editing files directly. The forked-subagent command is /subtask only when agent view is on, and /fork otherwise.

sheets.primary: Subagent: a reusable definition at .claude/agents/test-runner.md whose body is the system prompt instructing it to run the suite and return only the failing test names with their error messages, delegated to from the main session. This is the canonical subagent case, a side task whose logs would flood the main conversation.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Dynamic workflow. It loses because there is no loop, fan-out or cross-checking here for a script to make deterministic; one bounded delegated job is the cheaper primitive, and a workflow adds a run-approval prompt and a background runtime for a single command.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split, and the weaker half is the model's. The harness owns the hard part you asked for, the separate context window and the tools allowlist, but the model owns what it writes into the returned summary, so 'only the failures' is prompt guidance rather than an enforced filter.
sheets.context_boundary: The suite runs inside the subagent's own context window, where the tens of thousands of lines stay. Only the spawn prompt crosses in and only the subagent's returned summary crosses back to the main conversation; subagents report to the conversation that spawned them and to nothing else.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs when the main agent delegates on a description match or you invoke the agent explicitly, and it ends when the subagent returns its summary. Nothing persists between runs, and an interruption restarts the delegating turn rather than resuming the subagent.
sheets.failure_mode: It fails open and silently. The summary is the only artifact you ever see, so a summary that is too thin forces you to redo the work, a subagent that mis-invokes the suite can return a plausible 'all passed', and nothing structurally prevents it from pasting a large slab of raw output into its return; tool restriction, not the prompt, is the real control.
sheets.version_caveat: Subagents are stable with no enabling flag, plan restriction or experimental gate. The confirmed version note is operational: as of v2.1.198 /agents no longer opens a panel and instead prints the subagent file locations, and named background subagents show up in the @-mention typeahead with their status.

scenarios.scenario: One feature cuts across the frontend, the backend API, and the test suite. I want three workers, each owning one layer, keeping each other informed as the interface contract evolves during the work, and I want to drop into any individual worker directly to redirect it without going through an intermediary.

key.primary: Agent team: one teammate per layer, coordinating over direct messages and a shared task list, with each teammate a full session the user can open and message from the agent panel
key.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow with one stage per layer
key.rejection_reason: A workflow accepts no mid-run user input and its agents never converse; the plan is frozen in the script, so an interface change discovered by the backend agent cannot be negotiated with the frontend agent. Cross-layer coordination (frontend, backend, tests each owned by a different teammate) is one of the four documented strongest team use cases, and direct user-to-teammate interaction is exactly what teams add over every other mechanism.
key.lifecycle: explicit spawn request naming the three roles; requires the experimental env flag at session start
key.failure_mode: Two teammates editing the same file overwrite each other, since teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees; the work must be partitioned so each teammate owns different files, and coordination overhead plus token cost grow with team size.
key.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default; requires CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1

sheets.primary: An agent team with three named teammates, one per layer (frontend, backend API, tests), sharing a channel so interface contract changes propagate mid-flight, and each individually addressable so you can redirect one worker without going through a coordinator.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Three parallel subagents. Rejected on two counts specific to this request: subagents cannot exchange the evolving contract with each other, and once dispatched they are unaddressable, so redirecting one means stopping everything.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The harness provides addressability and the message bus; keeping the contract actually synchronized, and broadcasting a change rather than assuming it, is model discipline that nothing enforces.
sheets.context_boundary: Three separate context windows plus the shared team channel. What crosses is the messages teammates post and the files they write to the working tree; your direct redirect enters only the addressed teammate's window, which is precisely the property you asked for.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs for the duration of the feature and dissolves when the work lands or you tear the team down. There is no standing effect on later sessions and no persistence of the contract discussion beyond whatever the teammates wrote to files.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. The concrete risk is write collision and drift on the shared contract surface (types, API client, fixtures) that all three layers touch, since a shared working tree gives no isolation. A contract change that a teammate forgets to broadcast produces work that compiles in isolation and breaks on integration.
sheets.version_caveat: Agent teams are newer than subagents and I believe they are opt-in or experimental. I cannot confirm the version that introduced them, the enabling flag or setting, whether teammates share a working tree or get separate worktrees by default, or whether the feature is plan restricted.

sheets.primary: An agent team of three teammates, one owning the frontend, one the backend API, one the test suite, coordinated by the lead through the shared task list, with teammates messaging each other by name as the interface contract changes. Cross-layer changes spanning frontend, backend and tests are a documented strongest use case, and you steer any teammate directly from the agent panel.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagents. They report results back to the main agent only, never message each other, and cannot be opened and redirected mid-flight, which removes both of the properties this need is built around.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead assigns tasks or teammates self-claim them, and the lead judges when the contract is settled. Harness enforcement is available only through the TaskCreated, TaskCompleted and TeammateIdle hooks, and teammate permission prompts bubble up to the lead session for you to approve there.
sheets.context_boundary: Each teammate is an independent session with its own context window that loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills, plus the lead's spawn prompt, but not the lead's history. Contract changes cross as mailbox messages delivered automatically, as shared task-list state, and as files on disk; while you are viewing a teammate, plain text and skills go to that teammate but built-in commands still run in the lead's session.
sheets.lifecycle: The team forms at the first teammate spawn and is scoped to that session, one team per session with the lead fixed for its lifetime. You select a teammate with the arrow keys and press Enter to message it, Escape to interrupt its turn and 'x' to stop it; the team config directory is cleaned up when the session ends and in-process teammates are not restored by /resume.
sheets.failure_mode: The dominant risk here is file collision: agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so two teammates touching the same interface file overwrite each other, and the documented mitigation is partitioning files per teammate. It otherwise fails open, with task status lagging, the lead sometimes shutting down before the work is done, and teammates stopping on errors rather than recovering.
sheets.version_caveat: Experimental and disabled by default behind CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1. Direct interaction depends on display mode: the default is in-process since v2.1.179, split panes require tmux or iTerm2 with the it2 CLI and are unsupported in VS Code's integrated terminal, Windows Terminal and Ghostty, and the --teammate-mode flag is experimental and absent from claude --help.

sheets.primary: Agent team with three teammates, one owning the frontend, one the backend API and one the test suite, coordinating over the shared task list and direct peer messages as the interface contract evolves. Cross-layer coordination is a documented strongest case, and you address any teammate yourself from the agent panel (arrow keys to select, Enter to open its transcript and message it, Escape to interrupt) without going through the lead.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Subagent fan-out with three delegated layer workers. It loses on both stated requirements: subagents can only report back to the main agent and never message each other, and there is no way to converse with a running subagent to redirect it mid-task.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead is itself a Claude session deciding decomposition, assignment and integration, and nothing in the harness forces a teammate to broadcast a contract change; the shared task list, file-locked claiming and the TaskCreated/TaskCompleted/TeammateIdle hooks are the only harness-side levers.
sheets.context_boundary: Three fully independent sessions, each with its own context window, each loading CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills from project and user settings but not the lead's conversation history. Crossing the boundary: the spawn prompt, peer-to-peer messages, shared task state, your direct messages to a selected teammate, and the working tree itself.
sheets.lifecycle: The team exists from the first teammate spawn until shutdown or session exit, at which point the team config directory is removed automatically and the task list persists. Note that /resume and /rewind do not restore in-process teammates, so a resumed session may address teammates that no longer exist.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory, with file collision as the sharp edge: agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so two teammates touching the same interface or shared type file overwrite each other, which is exactly what a co-evolving contract invites. Task status also lags and blocks dependents, teammates stop on errors rather than recovering, and every teammate permission prompt bubbles up to the lead session.
sheets.version_caveat: Experimental and off by default behind CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1, on the v2.1.178 or later implicit lifecycle. Your ability to drop into a worker depends on display mode: teammateMode defaults to in-process since v2.1.179 (upgraded sessions no longer open split panes automatically), and split panes require tmux or iTerm2 with the it2 CLI and are unsupported in VS Code's integrated terminal, Windows Terminal and Ghostty.

sheets.primary: An agent team with three teammates, one per layer (frontend, backend API, tests), each given its own file ownership in the spawn prompt. They keep each other current on the evolving interface contract through direct teammate-to-teammate messaging and the shared task list, and you attach to any one of them from the agent panel (arrow keys, Enter) to redirect it without going through the lead.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A dynamic workflow. Rejected because a workflow moves the plan into a script that admits no mid-run user input and gives you nothing to attach to, so an interface contract that changes during the work cannot be renegotiated between workers or steered by you mid-flight.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The lead assigns and supervises, and each teammate decides what to tell the others; the harness only provides the mailbox, the file-locked task list, the attach-and-message panel, and hooks like `TaskCompleted` if you want a gate on work being marked done.
sheets.context_boundary: Three independent context windows plus the lead's. Each teammate loads CLAUDE.md, MCP servers and skills fresh and does not inherit the lead's history, so the contract has to travel explicitly: in the spawn prompt, in messages, in the shared task list, and in the code on disk. While you are viewing a teammate, your typed text and skills go to that teammate but built-in slash commands still execute in the lead's session.
sheets.lifecycle: The team exists from the first spawn until the teammates shut down or the lead's session ends; the team config directory is cleaned up automatically at session exit while the task list persists. A resumed session does not get its in-process teammates back, so a multi-day feature has to respawn them.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. Agent teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so any overlap in file ownership silently overwrites work; contract drift is only as good as the messages the teammates choose to send, and a teammate can code against a stale contract for a long time before anyone notices. Teammate permission prompts bubble up to the lead, so an unattended lead leaves workers stalled.
sheets.version_caveat: Experimental and off unless `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1` is set. Display defaults to in-process from v2.1.179 (before that it was `auto`); split panes need tmux or iTerm2 with the `it2` CLI and are not supported in the VS Code integrated terminal, Windows Terminal or Ghostty. Teammates do not inherit the lead's `/model` unless you set the default teammate model in `/config`, and their model is fixed at spawn.

scenarios.scenario: Run the strict type check, fix whatever it reports, run it again, and keep looping until it passes or two consecutive rounds make no progress. Nobody should babysit the loop or re-decide anything between rounds.

key.primary: Dynamic workflow: the script holds the check-fix-recheck loop and the deterministic two-rounds-no-progress termination condition
key.rejected_alternative: Chaining subagents turn by turn from the main conversation
key.rejection_reason: With chained subagents the model re-decides after every round and each round's results land in the main context, so a long loop both drifts (the stop condition is judgment, not code) and bloats context. The workflow docs give this exact prompt as a canonical shape ('keep fixing until a check passes... or two rounds in a row make no progress'): the script owns the iteration and the stop condition, and the session receives only the final outcome.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (per-round agents; loop state and round results held in script variables)
key.lifecycle: explicit invocation via the workflow request or ultracode keyword, or a saved command; approval prompt at launch
key.failure_mode: No mid-run user input, so if a fix genuinely needs a human call the run cannot pause to ask; a loop that stalls without triggering the stop condition burns agents toward the 1,000-agent per-run cap; exiting the session loses resumability.
key.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans; Pro enables via /config

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: Claude writes a script whose loop runs the strict type check, spawns agents to fix the reported errors, and re-runs the check, with the termination condition (passes, or two consecutive rounds with no progress) expressed in JavaScript. Save it afterwards so the same loop is a reusable command.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that instructs Claude to run the check, fix, and repeat. Rejected because then the loop and the stop rule are re-decided by the model every round, the whole transcript of every round accumulates in one context window, and 'no progress twice in a row' becomes a judgement call rather than a comparison of two counts.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime executes the loop and evaluates the stopping condition deterministically in script code, which is what removes the babysitting; the model owns only the per-round fixes inside each spawned agent.
sheets.context_boundary: The script executes in an isolated workflow runtime outside the conversation. Each round's raw type-check output and fix log stay in script variables and in the agents' own contexts; only the final result (passed, or stalled after N rounds) crosses back into the session.
sheets.lifecycle: Triggered by invoking the workflow (saved command, or the keyword in a prompt you typed). It runs in the background while the session stays responsive and ends when the script's own condition is satisfied, when you press `x`, or when a runtime cap trips. Resume works only within the same session.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed on iteration (the 1,000-agent cap makes an infinite loop impossible) but fails open on correctness: agents can make the check pass by weakening types or adding escape hatches, and the no-progress heuristic can halt with real errors outstanding. There is no mid-run input, so the only correction available is stopping the run.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan (Pro users must enable Dynamic workflows in `/config`). Note the permission behaviour: workflow subagents always run in `acceptEdits` and auto-approve file edits regardless of your session's permission mode, but shell commands outside your allowlist still prompt, so allowlist the type-check command up front or the unattended loop will sit waiting on you.

sheets.primary: Dynamic workflow holding the loop in script: run a checker agent, record the error count, spawn a fixer agent for what it reported, and repeat until the check passes or two consecutive rounds fail to reduce the count, saved to .claude/workflows/ as a rerunnable /<name> command. The docs describe this exact keep-fixing-until-it-passes shape as workflow work.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that documents the loop and lets the model run it. It loses because the round counter and the two-rounds-no-progress stopping rule become model judgment, so the model can stop early, keep grinding past the no-progress condition or re-choose its fix strategy between rounds, which is precisely what 'nobody re-decides anything between rounds' rules out.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime executes the script, so the loop, the comparison between rounds and the termination condition are code the model cannot reinterpret; only the content of each fix is model judgment, and each spawned agent runs in acceptEdits with your tool allowlist.
sheets.context_boundary: The loop runs in the workflow runtime, isolated from the conversation; each round's checker and fixer get their own context windows and the accumulating error lists stay in script variables. Only the final outcome returns to your context, so you never see the intermediate type-error dumps.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts on /<name> invocation, or on an explicit 'use a workflow'/ultracode opt-in for the first run, and it ends when the loop's own exit condition is met. It runs in the background while your session stays responsive and is resumable within the same session only.
sheets.failure_mode: It fails closed at parse time (a script the runtime cannot parse simply does not run) but fails open at runtime: an agent that dies resolves to null rather than throwing, and a naive progress comparison reads that as 'no new errors', so the loop can terminate early on a dead round or churn. There is also no mid-run user input, so nobody can correct a misdiagnosis in flight; the only intervention is stopping the run from /workflows.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later, on a paid plan, API, Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry, with Pro users enabling it from the Dynamic workflows row in /config. The workflowSizeGuideline setting (v2.1.202 or later, settable in any settings file from v2.1.219, default medium meaning fewer than 15 agents) is advice to Claude, not a cap, and the runtime caps still apply; /effort ultracode needs v2.1.203 or later.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow. The script holds the loop: run the strict type check, dispatch agents to fix what it reported, re-run the check, and terminate when it passes or when two consecutive rounds show no progress. The docs give this exact shape as a workflow example, keeping the checker, the fixes and the stop condition in code rather than in a conversation.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill describing the same loop. With a skill, Claude follows instructions and decides turn by turn whether to go around again, so the no-progress termination rule is reinterpreted every round and the loop is exactly the thing you end up supervising.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The workflow runtime executes the script, so the loop, the branching and the progress comparison are control flow rather than judgment; Claude only authors the script and receives the outcome. Nothing is re-decided between rounds because nothing is asked.
sheets.context_boundary: The script runs in the runtime's isolated environment, separate from your conversation. Each round's agents get their own context windows, and the type-check output and per-round error counts stay in script variables; only the final result crosses back into your session.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts when you ask for a workflow, use the ultracode keyword, or invoke a saved command, and runs in the background. It ends when the script's own condition is satisfied, when the 1,000-agent-per-run cap stops it, or when you stop it from /workflows; resume applies only within the same session.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed on interaction: there is no mid-run user input, only agent permission prompts can pause a run, so a bad fix strategy runs to completion before you can correct it, and the documented remedy is to run each stage as its own workflow when you want sign-off between stages. The script itself has no filesystem or shell access, so every edit goes through agents that run in acceptEdits with edits auto-approved, and a non-converging loop is bounded only by the agent cap.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan, with Pro users enabling the Dynamic workflows row in /config. The opt-in keyword is ultracode as of v2.1.160, where the literal trigger was previously 'workflow', and the keyword only counts as an opt-in when you type it yourself, not from -p, a scheduled task or a relayed webhook payload as of v2.1.210.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: a defined iterate-until-condition loop where the loop control lives outside the model. The harness (or an equivalent driver script built on the Agent SDK) owns the round counter and the stop predicate (type check clean, or two consecutive rounds with no reduction in error count), and the model only performs the fixes inside each round.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A skill that instructs the model to keep looping until the check passes. Rejected because the termination test then lives in model judgment, and the model will either stop early declaring victory or fail to notice the two-round no-progress condition.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness, for iteration and termination. The model owns only the per-round edits. That split is the whole point of the requirement that nobody re-decides anything between rounds.
sheets.context_boundary: Each round should run in a fresh or bounded context carrying forward only the current error list and the error count, so ten rounds of type checker output do not accumulate. Run inline in the main conversation instead, and every round stays resident and the loop degrades as context fills.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts on invocation, stops on the first clean run or on the second consecutive no-progress round, and applies to nothing outside that invocation. It is not a standing gate on commits or on future type errors.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open unless the stop condition is measured mechanically from the checker's own output. The classic failure is oscillation, where a fix for one error reintroduces another and the count plateaus without convergence. A subtler one: if progress is defined as raw error count, a refactor that consolidates many errors into one root error can look like no progress and stop the loop while real progress was happening.
sheets.version_caveat: I am not confident about the current name, file format, or release status of the dynamic-workflow mechanism in Claude Code, and it may be experimental or behind a flag. A shell or Agent SDK driven loop invoking Claude once per round is the version independent fallback that gives the same enforcement split.

scenarios.scenario: Migrate roughly 500 component files from one styling library to another. Every file gets the same transform, each performed in an isolated copy so edits never collide, and each result is verified before it counts as done.

key.primary: Dynamic workflow: discover the file list, fan out one transform agent per file working in an isolated copy, and run a verify step per result
key.rejected_alternative: An agent team splitting the migration among teammates
key.rejection_reason: Teams scale to a handful of long-running peers coordinated by a lead's turn-by-turn judgment, and teammates are not isolated in worktrees, so avoiding edit collisions means manually partitioning 500 files. A large identical-step migration is the workflow's documented home turf: dozens to hundreds of agents per run, per-item isolated copies, and a scripted verification stage; the docs give this exact 'migrate many files in parallel' prompt.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (per-file agents in isolated copies; results collected in script variables)
key.lifecycle: explicit invocation with the per-run approval prompt; savable as a command for later migration waves
key.failure_mode: Interrupting mid fan-out reruns every agent that started after the first unfinished one, even completed ones; the Large workflow warning (over 25 agents or 1.5M projected tokens) is advisory only and does not pause the run, so cost needs active watching.
key.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans; Pro enables via /config

sheets.primary: Dynamic workflow: pipeline() over the roughly 500 component paths passed in as args, each item running a transform agent with worktree isolation so parallel edits cannot collide, then a verify agent before the item counts as done, saved as a reusable /<name> command. Discovery happens outside the script or in a first-stage agent, since a workflow has no direct filesystem access of its own.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The /batch skill, which splits one large change into worktree-isolated subagents that each open a pull request. It loses on scale and on ownership: it is sized for 5 to 30 subagents rather than 500 files, and the model still holds the plan turn by turn, so the identical-transform-plus-verify contract is not guaranteed per file.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime owns the per-item loop, the isolation and the ordering of transform then verify; the model only decides what each transform looks like. Workflow-spawned agents run in acceptEdits with your tool allowlist regardless of your session's permission mode, so file edits inside the run are auto-approved.
sheets.context_boundary: The script runs in the workflow runtime; each file's agent has its own context window and its own isolated checkout, so no agent sees another's edits. Per-file verdicts stay in script variables and only the final collected summary crosses into your conversation, with the actual changes crossing through the filesystem.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts on invocation and each item runs transform then verify independently, with no barrier between stages, ending when every item has passed through. Resume is in-session only, and the replay rule matters at this size: cached results stop at the first agent that did not finish, so every agent that started after it reruns even if it completed.
sheets.failure_mode: The hard cap is the real hazard: 1,000 agents per run and 16 concurrent (fewer on machines with limited CPU cores) means 500 files times a transform plus a verify stage sits exactly at the ceiling, so any discovery agent or retry pushes the run over and it must be batched. Beyond that it fails open, since a failed agent null-fills rather than throwing and a short result set reads as 'fewer files needed migrating'.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan (Pro enables it in /config), or API, Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry. A run this size trips the advisory Large workflow warning at more than 25 scheduled agents or a projected 1.5 million tokens, which requires v2.1.203 or later and does not pause or limit anything.

sheets.primary: Parallel subagents, one per file or small batch, each operating in its own git worktree so writes cannot collide, dispatched by a skill (or dynamic workflow) that owns the queue, a fixed worker pool, the per-result verification command, and the merge back.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Rejected because 500 identical transforms require no negotiation between workers; a team buys addressability and chat that this task never uses, at real coordination and token cost.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Split. The harness owns the isolation (separate contexts, separate worktrees) and owns the verification verdict if the check is a real command whose exit code gates the result. The model owns transform quality and, dangerously, owns whether every file actually got attempted.
sheets.context_boundary: Each subagent sees only its assigned files and returns a pass/fail plus a short diff summary. The orchestrating context holds the queue and a results ledger, never 500 files of component source. Merge conflicts surface at the worktree level, not in anyone's context.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs once per migration invocation and ends when the queue drains and all worktrees are merged or discarded. The skill persists for reruns; the workers, worktrees, and their contexts do not.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. Expect conflicts on the shared files every worker wants to touch (theme config, global styles, the styling library's provider setup), silent skips counted as done, and per-file verification that passes while the application is broken in aggregate because no worker sees the composition. There is also a resource hazard if concurrency scales with file count instead of a fixed worker pool.
sheets.version_caveat: Git worktree isolation and background or parallel agent execution are relatively recent Claude Code additions and I do not know the version that introduced either. Worktree isolation also presupposes a git repository with a clean working tree, and I do not know the current ceiling on simultaneously running agents.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: the script discovers the component files, then uses `pipeline()` to run one migration agent per file in its own isolated checkout (a worktree), followed by a verification step per file before the result counts as done. Saving the script makes the migration repeatable and inspectable.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The `/batch` skill, which is the packaged subagent-plus-worktree pattern that splits a change into roughly 5 to 30 worktree-isolated subagents each opening a pull request. Rejected because 500 files far exceeds that fan-out, the per-file verification gate is not part of that pattern, and a pull request per slice is the wrong output shape here.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime owns the fan-out, the isolation of each unit of work, and the fact that a verify agent runs after each transform; the model owns the transform itself and the verdict each verifier reaches.
sheets.context_boundary: The orchestration runs in the workflow runtime, separate from the conversation. Each file's agent has its own context window and its own checkout, so the file contents and diffs never enter the main session; only the aggregated result of the run crosses back.
sheets.lifecycle: Starts on invocation, runs in the background, ends when the script returns or you stop it. If you stop mid fan-out, only agents that finished before the first unfinished one return from cache; every agent that started after it reruns, which is why a many-small-agents shape preserves more progress than a few long ones.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. 'Verified' is a model verdict per file, not a test run, so a subtly wrong migration can be marked done; and because each file is transformed in an isolated copy, the real risk is the merge back, where cross-file conventions and shared theme files drift out of sync. Unallowlisted shell commands can also stall a very long run on a prompt.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan (Pro enables it in `/config`). Runtime caps apply: at most 16 concurrent agents (fewer on machines with limited CPU cores) and 1,000 agents total per run, which 500 files plus 500 verifiers essentially exhausts, so plan on slicing by directory. Also raise `workflowSizeGuideline` (v2.1.202 or later, default `medium` from v2.1.219) or Claude will aim far too small.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: one phase discovers the component files, a pipeline() fans out one transform agent per file with each agent working in its own isolated copy so edits never collide, and a verification step checks each result before it counts as done. The docs give the 500-file migration in isolated copies as a canonical workflow example.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The bundled /batch skill. It is the nearest packaged form of the same idea, worktree-isolated subagents, but it splits a change into 5 to 30 subagents that each open a pull request, which is an order of magnitude short of 500 files and gives no per-file verification gate.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness for orchestration and sequencing: the runtime executes the script, so the per-file fan-out and the verify-before-done gate are script stages, not requests. The isolation itself is still performed by the agents, because the script has no filesystem access of its own.
sheets.context_boundary: The script runs in the runtime's isolated environment; each per-file agent has its own context window and its own checkout of the code, and per-file results are held in script variables. Only the final summary crosses into your conversation.
sheets.lifecycle: It starts on invocation, by asking for a workflow or by running the saved command, and runs in the background with progress visible in /workflows. It ends when the script returns, when a cap is reached, or when you stop it; resume is limited to the same session, and exiting Claude Code restarts the run from scratch.
sheets.failure_mode: Scale is where it hurts: 16 concurrent agents means 500 files run in many waves, and stopping mid fan-out is expensive because on resume only cached results before the first unfinished agent survive, and every agent that started after it runs again even if it completed. It fails open on correctness, since the script cannot touch files itself and depends on each agent honouring its isolated copy and on the verify agent actually catching a bad transform.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan, with Pro enabling Dynamic workflows in /config, and 1,000 agents per run is a hard runtime cap for a job this size. The workflow size guideline defaults to medium as of v2.1.219, which aims Claude at fewer than 15 agents, so a 500-file migration needs large or unrestricted set in /config or the workflowSizeGuideline setting.

scenarios.scenario: A 60-file pull request needs a correctness review of every changed file, one reviewer per file, then all per-file findings merged, deduplicated, and ranked into a single summary. The reviewers have nothing to discuss with each other; only the merged output matters.

key.primary: Dynamic workflow: fan out one reviewer agent per changed file, then hand all findings to a single merge agent that ranks and deduplicates
key.rejection_reason: Parallel code review is a documented team use case, which makes this a genuine near-miss, but the team version splits review by lens (security, performance, coverage) across a few peers who share and challenge each other's findings. Here reviewers are per-file, the docs' team comparison says to choose based on whether workers need to communicate (these do not), 60 workers exceeds the 3-to-5 teammate guidance, and the merge is a deterministic collect-and-reduce step; the docs list this exact 'review every changed file and write one summary' workflow shape.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (per-file reviewer agents; findings flow through script variables to the merge agent)
key.lifecycle: explicit invocation; naturally saved as a command to rerun on every branch
key.failure_mode: The single merge agent gates the whole deliverable, so weak deduplication or ranking buries valid per-file findings; a stopped run reruns all agents that started after the first unfinished one on resume.
key.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later; paid plans; Pro enables via /config

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: one `agent()` per changed file through `pipeline()` for the correctness review, then a single synthesis agent that receives all per-file findings and returns one deduplicated, ranked summary. Save it as a command so the same review runs on every branch.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Rejected because inter-agent messaging and a shared task list are the entire cost of a team and this task explicitly needs none of it, and 60 teammates is an order of magnitude past the 3 to 5 range where teams stay manageable.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The script guarantees each changed file gets exactly one reviewer and that exactly one merge step runs over the complete finding set; the model owns the review content and the ranking judgement.
sheets.context_boundary: Runs in the workflow runtime. Each reviewer sees only its own file in its own context, the per-file findings accumulate in script variables rather than in your session, and they are handed to the merge agent as script data. Only the final ranked summary enters the conversation's context window.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs when the workflow command is invoked against the pull request, in the background, ending when the summary is returned. It applies only to that run; nothing persists between runs except the saved script itself.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open, with a specific blind spot: a reviewer that sees one file in isolation cannot see cross-file or interface-level defects, so the class of bug a 60-file pull request most often contains is the class this shape misses. The dedupe step is also a single model pass that can quietly drop a genuine finding while collapsing near-duplicates.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan; Pro users enable it in `/config`, and an organisation can disable it via managed settings. If you want this to fire on every pull request without a human invoking it, that is a different surface (GitHub Actions or GitHub code review), not a workflow gate. In `claude -p` and the Agent SDK there is no launch approval prompt, so the run starts immediately.

sheets.primary: A dynamic workflow: a pipeline() that runs one reviewer agent per changed file, followed by a single merge phase where one agent receives all per-file findings and returns a deduplicated, ranked summary. The docs list this exact review-every-changed-file-then-merge shape as a workflow example.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Teammates exist to share a task list, message each other and challenge each other's findings, which is pure coordination overhead and a higher token bill when the reviewers have nothing to discuss and only the merged output matters.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The runtime executes the script, so the one-reviewer-per-file fan-out and the single merge stage are guaranteed structure rather than a plan Claude re-derives, and the number of reviewers is not subject to turn-by-turn judgment.
sheets.context_boundary: Each reviewer has its own context window holding only its one file; all 60 finding sets live in script variables inside the runtime's isolated environment. Only the merged, ranked summary crosses into your conversation.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs when invoked, either through a saved command or by asking for a workflow, executes in the background with per-phase progress in /workflows, and stops when the merge phase returns. It is resumable within the same session only, and stopping it loses the work of any agent that started after the first unfinished one.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open on review quality. Nothing forces a reviewer to find anything, and a merge agent given 60 finding sets can drop or mis-rank items, so an empty or thin report is indistinguishable from a clean diff unless the script adds a verification phase. Operationally it is capped at 16 concurrent agents, and shell or MCP calls outside your allowlist can still stop the run to prompt you mid-review.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later and a paid plan, with Pro turning on Dynamic workflows in /config, and it can be disabled per user with disableWorkflows or org-wide through managed settings. A run of about 60 agents crosses the 25-agent threshold that triggers the advisory Large workflow warning introduced in v2.1.203.

sheets.primary: Parallel subagents: one read-only reviewer subagent per changed file, each returning a structured finding list against a fixed schema, followed by a single merge step (in the orchestrator or in one dedicated synthesizer subagent) that deduplicates and ranks.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Rejected because the scenario states the reviewers have nothing to discuss; the team's message bus and addressability would add cost and noise while changing nothing about the merged output.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. Nothing at the harness level guarantees that all 60 files were actually reviewed or that the merge preserved every finding, unless the file list is enumerated by a script and the ledger is reconciled against it.
sheets.context_boundary: Each reviewer's window holds one file's diff plus whatever context it pulls; only its findings cross back. The parent then holds 60 finding lists at once, which is itself a large payload, so a capped and structured per-reviewer output matters as much as the isolation does.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs on invocation against one specific pull request or diff and ends with the merged summary. It carries no standing state and must be re-run per pull request; it is not a merge gate unless something else enforces it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails open. The structural cost of the isolation is that cross-file defects are invisible by construction: a caller and callee contract broken across two files is never seen by any single reviewer. Deduplication can also collapse two genuinely different findings into one, and 60 parallel dispatches is a real token and rate-limit expense.
sheets.version_caveat: Subagents are generally available, but I do not know the current limit on how many can run concurrently, so 60 will very likely be queued in waves rather than run simultaneously. Wall-clock expectations should assume batching.

sheets.primary: Dynamic workflow: fan out one reviewer agent per changed file, collect all 60 result objects behind a barrier, then hand the whole set to a single merge agent that deduplicates and ranks the findings into one summary. This is the documented review-every-changed-file-and-write-one-summary shape.
sheets.rejected_alternative: Agent team with per-file reviewer teammates. It loses because the reviewers explicitly have nothing to say to each other, so the only thing a team adds over a script is coordination overhead, a separate Claude session's token cost per reviewer, and file-collision risk that buys nothing.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. The script owns the one-reviewer-per-file fan-out and the barrier before the merge stage, so coverage is a loop over the changed-file list rather than a promise; the model owns only each review's judgment and the ranking heuristic inside the merge prompt.
sheets.context_boundary: All 60 reviews happen in the workflow runtime, each in its own agent context window, and the per-file finding sets live in script variables. Only the single merged, deduplicated, ranked summary crosses into your conversation.
sheets.lifecycle: It runs on /<name> invocation or an explicit workflow opt-in and ends when the merge agent returns. The merge stage is the one place a barrier is required, so it must wait for every reviewer to return rather than streaming per item as pipeline() would.
sheets.failure_mode: It fails open at the join: a reviewer that dies resolves to null, so the merged summary silently covers 57 of 60 files and reads exactly like a complete review; filter the results and assert the count against the changed-file list. If the fan-out is written with pipeline() instead of a barrier, the merge can also run on a partial finding set.
sheets.version_caveat: Requires Claude Code v2.1.154 or later on a paid plan, API, Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry; Pro enables it in /config. The default medium size guideline aims at fewer than 15 agents but is advice rather than a cap, so a 60-reviewer run still schedules and merely raises the advisory Large workflow warning above 25 agents on v2.1.203 or later.

scenarios.scenario: Three specialists must run in strict sequence: one finds performance issues, one fixes exactly what was found, one verifies the fixes. Each step consumes the previous step's output, and all three work in the same handful of hot files.

key.primary: Chain subagents in sequence within one session: the main agent runs each specialist and passes the relevant results to the next
key.rejected_alternative: An agent team with three specialist teammates
key.rejection_reason: The three-specialists framing suggests peers, but the steps are strictly dependent and touch the same files. The team docs say exactly that: for sequential tasks, same-file edits, or work with many dependencies, a single session or subagents are more effective, and concurrent teammates editing the same files overwrite each other. The subagent docs document this chaining pattern directly ('use the code-reviewer subagent to find issues, then the optimizer subagent to fix them'), giving each specialist isolation while the caller carries forward only the needed context.
key.context_boundary: isolated context (each subagent starts fresh; the main agent relays results between steps)
key.lifecycle: model-decided delegation, steered by naming the subagents in the prompt
key.failure_mode: Handoff loss: the main agent summarizes between steps, so detail the next specialist needed can be dropped; each returned result also accumulates in the main context across the chain.

sheets.primary: Three custom subagent definitions, a finder, a fixer and a verifier, invoked in strict sequence by the main session, which passes each step's returned summary into the next step's prompt. The docs point sequential, dependency-heavy, same-file work at a single session or subagents rather than any parallel coordination style.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An agent team. Teams do not isolate teammates in worktrees, so three peers editing the same handful of hot files overwrite each other, and the shared task list adds coordination cost for work that is a straight chain with no discussion.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The model. The main session decides when a step is finished and what to hand forward, so the strict ordering is a prompt-level promise rather than a runtime guarantee. If the order must hold every time, that belongs in a hook, because an instruction is a request while a PreToolUse hook that blocks is enforcement.
